During the preliminary design review (PDR), three design alternatives were presented, each representing a design on a spectrum of basic to full capabilities, and their associated costs were estimated. After a down-selection process, DOE selected the full capabilities alternative (Option 1), including the grid simulator. Consequently, during the final design phase of this project, this option was developed in detail, and it is the one described in this document. Final Technical Report 10/57 2 MTV GENERAL DESCRIPTION The primary concept behind the project is to create a flexible CEC testing platform suitable for various environments, such as rivers, estuaries, and open ocean, and capable of accommodating different sizes of CECs, ranging from 3 to 8 meters in diameter. MTV is a non-propelled catamaran barge, providing inherent transverse stability due to its double hull configuration. Longitudinal pitching performance is enhanced by incorporating a water ballast system. The vessel is composed of two rigid platforms connecting both hulls, staying above the water at all times to facilitate equipment installation and support control room and container housing sensitive instrumentation. The CEC deployment mechanism involves a supporting structure linking both hulls with a central pile capable of vertical displacement using a rack and pinion jack-up system. This allows for adaptable turbine depths, with a maximum depth of 6 m below the keel for the central axis of the turbine, in the case of a horizontal axis turbine (HATT). A modular design ensures the subsystem's removal if necessary. An overview of the MTV is depicted in Figure 2-1. Figure 2-1 General view of the MTV The MTV will operate with a sliding deck on two rails within each hull, facilitating horizontal movement under the supporting structure for turbine installation and supporting the CEC during towing. Additionally, an A-frame will be installed at the fore of the MTV for tests where the turbine hangs from the vessel. Final Technical Report 11/57 The MTV’s mooring offers three options for adapting to different water depths. In shallow areas, four jack-up legs can elevate the vessel above the water. Intermediate depths, such as those found in estuaries and some open ocean locations, can utilize a 4-point catenary line mooring system composed of chains and drag anchors. For deeper ocean locations, pad eyes will allow connection to a preinstalled external mooring system. Power for the MTV will come from two gensets, with load banks for power dissipation during testing. A grid simulator system will also be integrated. Electrical and control-related equipment will be divided between the hulls' inner compartments and a container on the aft platform for vessel control, including NREL’s MODAQ system for data management. Transportation will occur via towing with a tug vessel or, for long-distance trips, on a heavy-lifting ship using cranes. Figure 2-2 depicts the MTV with Jack-up legs and the deployed CEC.
